sources.title: Microsoft to expand Maia chip for the AI era
sources.text: Oct 12, 2026 | Scott Guthrie - Executive Vice President, Cloud + AI As we move into the era of Super Intelligence, Microsoft is entering a new phase of infrastructure. We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services. The multigenerational Azure Maia program has become a foundational element of Microsoft’s AI infrastructure strategy. Maia 200 is now serving Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft Copilot , and supporting the MAI team as they develop next-generation models, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by end of year. Across these workloads, Maia 200 runs OpenAI models , Microsoft’s own MAI models and leading open-source model families. Insights from the scale of Microsoft’s AI services allow for unique co-design between hardware systems and software applications to optimize real-world use cases across enterprise applications and industry scenarios. Maia 300 is a complete intelligent system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks. By improving efficiency across the system, we expect Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems. And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200. The Azure Maia system is designed around the real-world workloads Microsoft runs at scale and the models we expect to build in the years ahead. Because silicon development takes years, our software and hardware teams collaborate early to anticipate architectures, scale and capabilities, translating those requirements into greater memory capacity, higher bandwidth and more accelerators operating as a single system. That co-engineering is already delivering measurable efficiency gains. Maia 200 is deploying across the United States, Europe and Australia and delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt for built-in AI capabilities in Microsoft Teams, Copilot and Cowork experiences compared with leading GPU infrastructure. Experience running our AI models and services on Maia 200 directly informed the design of Maia 300. Together, the two generations are designed to support a broad set of additional Microsoft’s AI services: multi-step agentic work that will help GitHub deliver coding experiences more efficiently; cloud-scale model serving that will help Microsoft Foundry support diverse architectures and deployment environments; inference and data generation for the MAI team; and latency-sensitive interactions that will help Dragon Copilot scale workflows and reduce clinicians’ administrative burden. AI is becoming a foundational layer of every application, workflow and business process. As enterprises move beyond chat experiences to systems of agents that can reason, act and collaborate, AI infrastructure must deliver intelligence securely and efficiently at scale while continuously adapting as models and workloads evolve. As the third generation of our Azure Maia program, Maia 300 is designed with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads. This involves balancing compute, memory bandwidth, networking and power efficiency at cloud scale. Key capabilities of the Maia 300 system include: Less data movement, more useful compute: Moving data efficiently, rather than raw compute power, is increasingly the bottleneck in large inference systems. Maia 300’s software-defined dataflow architecture and AI-assisted kernel optimization work together to maximize locality, reduce data movement and improve utilization across compute, memory and networking resources. By treating dataflow as a first-class design principle, Maia 300 delivers a significant performance-per-watt advantage over traditional GPU architectures. Higher memory bandwidth within every watt: As AI workloads become increasingly context and memory-bound, Maia 300 delivers industry-leading HBM bandwidth per watt. Eight HBM4 stacks provide 18.0 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth within a 950-watt TDP, enabling efficient execution of large models and long-context workloads. Specialized kernel support uses on-die SRAM as a software-managed scratchpad, reducing pressure on HBM. Chiplet architecture for enhanced efficiency: A new multi-chiplet architecture separates compute, memory-controller and I/O functions, improving efficiency, scalability and cost structure. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC’s N2P process node to maximize performance-per-watt. Larger context, richer intelligence: By designing for advanced low-precision formats, including enhanced MXFP4, Maia 300 reduces memory and bandwidth requirements for both computation and KV-cache storage. The result is larger context windows, higher throughput and improved model efficiency within the same power envelope. Scale-up networking at datacenter scale: Maia 300 treats networking as a seamless extension of the software-defined dataflow architecture. Rather than moving data through separate communication layers, dataflow operations span compute, memory and network resources as a single system. High-bandwidth interconnects between Maia accelerators are optimized for tensor parallelism, while a custom AI transport delivers performant and reliable scale-up communication across accelerators and racks. The AI-optimized transport leverages Ethernet-based networking infrastructure to enable a unified topology that scales efficiently from a single rack to datacenter-scale deployments. Higher AI throughput from every rack: Maia 300 rack systems bring together 96 accelerators within a 167-kilowatt power envelope, delivering 27.6 TB of HBM capacity and 1.7 PB/s of aggregate HBM bandwidth across a high-speed scale-up domain. sources.title: Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs
sources.text: The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027. Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services. Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie , executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.” These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services,” says Guthrie. Maia 300 is a successor to the 200, which was only announced in January . Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models. “Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.” Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team. Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”

stories.title: Share GPU clusters across teams with isolation and fairness using Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
stories.summary: A reference architecture for securely sharing one Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS cluster across multiple teams, using AWS IAM Identity Center for authentication, per-team SageMaker Domains and Kubernetes namespaces for isolation, HyperPod Task Governance for fairness, and namespace-level cost allocation for chargeback.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Share GPU clusters across teams with isolation and fairness using Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
sources.text: Multiple teams within the same company increasingly need shared access to expensive GPU clusters for their generative AI operations, while maintaining isolation boundaries, resource fairness, and operational independence. Consider a data science team training large language models, a computer vision group running inference workloads, and a research team experimenting with new model architectures. All of them might need access to the same cluster. Without a well-designed multi-tenant (multi-team) architecture, organizations face uncontrolled resource consumption, weak isolation between teams, an inability to attribute shared GPU costs to the teams that incur them, and administrative overhead that slows down innovation. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod is a purpose-built AI service that simplifies the management of large-scale compute clusters for gen AI workloads. It provides resilient, optimized clusters orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) or Slurm, so organizations can run distributed training, interactive development, and model inference at scale. At the same time, it automatically handles node health monitoring, fault recovery, and cluster lifecycle management. In this post, we present a reference architecture for building a multi-tenant environment on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with EKS. This architecture uses AWS IAM Identity Center for centralized authentication, per-team SageMaker AI domains for a tailored user experience, Kubernetes namespaces for workload isolation, HyperPod Task Governance for fair resource allocation, and namespace-level cost allocation for per-team spend visibility and chargeback. By the end of this post, you will have a clear blueprint for multiple teams to efficiently share a single HyperPod EKS cluster. The following diagram illustrates the high-level architecture of a multi-tenant HyperPod EKS deployment. In this example, two teams (Team A and Team B) share a single HyperPod EKS cluster, each operating within their own isolated namespace. Figure 1: High-level multi-tenant architecture for two teams sharing one HyperPod EKS cluster The architecture is structured as a layered flow from left to right, connecting user identity through authorization controls and into isolated workload namespaces on the cluster. On the far left, individual users from each team (User 1 from Team A, User 2 from Team B) interact with the system through two paths. Both paths authenticate through the AWS IAM Identity Center Portal, which federates with an external identity provider (such as Microsoft Entra ID) shown at the bottom-left. The first path is through CLI access. Users authenticate with aws sso login , which redirects them to the Identity Center portal, and then obtain temporary credentials from their team’s permission set to submit tasks directly to the EKS cluster with kubectl . In the diagram, the pink arrow flows from the CLI terminal across the top directly into the HyperPod EKS cluster. The second path is through the Identity Center portal directly, where users select the SageMaker Studio application to sign in to their team-specific SageMaker AI domain. Each team has a corresponding permission set (TeamA permission set, TeamB permission set) that carries the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies needed for CLI workflows. Identity Center automatically provisions an IAM role for each permission set, shown in the diagram as TeamA-permissionset-role and TeamB-permissionset-role (labeled “CLI/Console role”). This role serves as the IAM principal when users authenticate through aws sso login . From the Identity Center portal, users are routed to their team-specific SageMaker AI domain. Each domain (SageMaker AI domain Team A and SageMaker AI domain Team B) provides a dedicated Amazon SageMaker Studio GUI and is configured with a team-specific execution role ( TeamA-role and TeamB-role respectively). These domains serve as the primary workspace interface, so users can submit tasks from the GUI (shown by the pink arrows flowing toward EKS). At the EKS boundary, access entries map IAM roles to Kubernetes permissions. The diagram shows access entries for TeamA-role and TeamB-role (the Studio execution roles), which authorize requests originating from the SageMaker Studio GUI. Access entries must also be configured for the Identity Center-provisioned CLI/Console roles ( TeamA-permissionset-role and TeamB-permissionset-role ) to authorize requests arriving through kubectl . All access entries are associated with managed or custom role-based access control (RBAC) policies (represented by the key icon) and scoped to the team’s designated namespace. As a result, whether access originates from Studio or the CLI, users can only interact with resources in their own namespace. The cluster itself is depicted with two cross-cutting platform layers at the top: HyperPod Observability (for monitoring and dashboards) and HyperPod Task Governance (for compute quota management and scheduling priorities). Below these layers, the cluster is partitioned into Namespace A (Team A) and Namespace B (Team B). Within each namespace, teams can run their own HyperPod Spaces (interactive development environments), HyperPod PyTorch jobs (distributed training workloads), and HyperPod Inference endpoints (model serving). Beneath the cluster, the architecture includes two storage tiers. The first is a POSIX-compliant file system (Amazon FSx for Lustre or Amazon FSx for OpenZFS) organized into per-team shared directories ( /fsx/TeamA , /fsx/TeamB ) and per-user home directories ( /home/User1 , /home/User2 ). The second is per-team or shared Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets for object storage, governed by the team’s IAM execution role. This architecture isolates each team from authentication through authorization to workload execution, while sharing expensive GPU infrastructure efficiently. sources.title: Impactful scheduling for GPU clusters
sources.text: Building a cluster scheduler to prioritize high-impact research while maintaining full occupancy On the AI Infrastructure team at Ai2, we’re responsible for providing the institute’s GPU compute capacity, specifically targeting large, distributed training workloads. We think about this task as a pyramid of four metrics that build on each other. The foundation is availability : how often the hardware is healthy and ready for work. Above this is occupancy : the fraction of available time assigned to a specific workload. Next is impact : how often the most valuable workloads are chosen to receive resources. The capstone of the pyramid is utilization : the fraction of GPU capacity used over the lifetime of a workload. This post is about improving the impact of our scheduling decisions. We recently replaced a priority-based scheduler with a system including GPU time budgets, hierarchical fair-share allocation, and a time-slicing contract. As a result, we shifted the debate about how much GPU time each research project deserves from a case-by-case operational task to a transparent administrative budgeting process. At Ai2, we manage thousands of NVIDIA H100, B200, and B300 GPUs arranged in clusters ranging in size from 88 to 1024 GPUs. These clusters are built for large-scale distributed training of AI models, and they serve a group of about 150 internal researchers whose work covers a diverse set of AI domains, including the full model flow of LLM and VLM training, robotics reinforcement learning (RL) simulation, and post-training for scientific agentic use cases. Like many labs, we have demand for GPU time that far exceeds supply. Based on submitted workloads, at any moment in time we have outstanding requests for 2-3x more GPUs than are available. One way to think about this is that every available GPU hour on our cluster has 2-3 different research workloads competing for it. Historically, we used a priority-based scheduler, and we allowed workloads to opt out of preemptability. Each team had a limit on concurrent GPUs that could be used by workloads which were protected from preemption. Preemptible workloads could exceed that limit on idle GPUs. This strategy produced predictable pathologies. For example, we observed instances of GPU “squatting” where users would park no-op workloads they could connect to when the need arose. This occurred because researchers found they could not launch debugging workloads with low enough latency to tackle problems in real time. We also observed priority inflation, where eventually 100% of scheduled workloads used HIGH priority. This meant that lower priority levels were starved of GPU time altogether. Since preemptability was optional, we also found that our on-call engineers spent a majority of their ticket response time negotiating the organized shutdown of non-preemptable workloads running on hosts with known maintenance problems. When these problems emerged, we were slow to identify their root causes. Our initial attempts to ensure the most important work received GPU time were focused on tighter control of how priorities were set, and, ultimately, working around the priority-based scheduler by explicitly assigning GPU monopolies to important projects. While we didn’t recognize it at first, we had built a perfect laboratory for observing the “tragedy of the commons.” Individuals were competing over a scarce, shared resource and, by seeking to maximize individual outcomes, achieving a non-optimal global result and abusing the underlying resource. We were far from the first to observe this kind of interaction. Resource allocation is a fascinating research domain that mixes algorithm development, economics, and system management. A central problem is that users often know the value of their own jobs better than the organization does, but they may have incentives to hide that value or hold on to resources even when doing so hurts total performance. For example, in their 2011 paper introducing Dominant Resource Fairness , Ghodsi et al. recount an anecdote in which a search company provided dedicated machines to jobs only if their users could guarantee high utilization. They soon discovered “users would sprinkle their code with infinite loops to artificially inflate utilization levels.” The hardware changes, but the fundamental problems that make resource allocation complex persist. The classic solution to a tragedy of the commons is to privatize the shared resource—owners are incentivized to maximize the value of their property. When we assigned teams monopolies over sets of GPUs, we were already doing a version of this, but it was too coarse. It caused GPUs to sit idle due to the seasonality of research. Teams are ready to run experiments and training at different times, so assigning a monopoly would ensure that there would be times when no jobs were ready to execute, with another team left waiting for capacity. We were manually solving a knapsack problem , trying to fit dynamically changing research needs into a static schedule. We wanted the ownership incentive, but we also wanted to maintain full occupancy of the GPUs. We decided to iterate on the ownership model. Instead of issuing teams GPUs, we chose to allocate a portion of GPU time. Predicting demand into the future would require knowing the result of novel science experiments, so it cannot be forecast with precision. Priority across research efforts, however, is a question of strategy, and it can be more easily debated and decided in advance. Instead of trying to solve the scheduling puzzle, we enabled leadership to think like investors. Before the workloads exist, decide how to fund each research effort with GPU time based on their judgment of its likely impact. The scheduler could then use that information when prioritizing arriving workloads. With this in mind, we devised a hierarchical system where managers could proportionally allocate GPU time to the projects and researchers they were respon

sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Cyber-attack similar to OpenAI Medicare breach seems likely in UK, says minister
sources.text: Kanishka Narayan, concerned by Australian incident, says British cyber defences could be bypassed by artificial intelligence agent An AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the OpenAI breach of Australia’s healthcare system is likely, “if not inevitable”, in the UK, according to a senior minister. Kanishka Narayan, the UK AI minister, indicated that the British government’s own cyber defences would be bypassed by a technology that has developed highly sophisticated skills in cybersecurity. In a speech Narayan said an incident in June when an OpenAI agent – a computer program acting autonomously – infiltrated Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system, could be repeated in the UK. “It concerns me,” he said. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached.” Narayan said the agent’s task was “benign” as it searched for information about public spending on medicines, but it nonetheless went after data that it was not authorised to have. “The Australian government has said that no personal medical records are known to have been accessed, and there is no evidence of wider compromise, but the incident should concern us,” he said. Speaking at a science and tech hub at Imperial College London, Narayan said the security minister, Dan Jarvis, would lead a government programme to strengthen against cyber-attacks, including from AI. The government will also consider using the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill as a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents. Narayan spoke before a parliamentary hearing on AI safety on Tuesday into the issue . Senior figures from OpenAI and Anthropic will be among those giving evidence to MPs on the business, innovation, science and trade committee. They will also be joined by the head of the UK’s AI Security Institute, Henry de Zoete. Narayan confirmed that the institute would gain access to advanced AI models before they were released, after the White House had reportedly placed restrictions on their availability. “I can confirm that AI scientists at the AI Security Institute are now conducting rigorous evaluations of the latest generations of models, including [Google’s] Gemini … to identify risks early to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe,” he said. The minister added that leading AI companies must “listen” to warnings of safety risks posed by their technology – and not release models if they carried a serious threat. “And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: listen when your scientists warn of severe dangers; investigate unexpected behaviours; and if you can’t adequately control the risks, do not release the system,” he said. “I want the labs to be honest.” Narayan said the UK would “play its part” in coordinating an international response to AI safety by making the technology a “central focus” of Britain’s G20 presidency next year. “We know that these challenges cannot be addressed by a single country alone, but by virtue of our capability, by virtue of the foundations of our trust, Britain will play its part,” he said.

sources.title: UK cyber defenses ‘likely’ to be breached, warns AI minister
sources.text: Kanishka Narayan wants more to be done about unauthorized AI agents activity UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan has warned that it is “likely, if not inevitable” that the nation's cyber defenses will be breached by AI agents. Narayan’s warning comes after numerous frontier models have escaped testing environments and hacked third party companies, including one case where an OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June 2026. Speaking at a press conference, Narayan also said that AI companies should, “Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system.” The AI minister also revealed that the UK government is planning to use advanced AI to counter the threats posed by AI, which will build upon two pilot programs that have helped spot and patch over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems. In addition, frontier AI systems are undergoing “rigorous evaluations” by the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI), in order to “identify risks early” and “test robust safeguards to help keep people safe.” However, there have been some roadblocks in AISI’s ability to test some of the latest models. In September 2026, US President Donald Trump asked OpenAI and Anthropic to not share their latest models with UK testers until US labs had conducted their own testing. Narayan said that the UK government has since worked with the White House, “to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released" (via BBC ). Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! AI protections are also likely to be introduced as part of the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, Narayan said, with a particular focus on regulations surrounding the reporting and disclosure of AI incidents. “It's promising to see the Government taking frontier AI cyber defences seriously,” said Richard Wainwright, Field CTO, EMEA at Okta. “As AI agents become more autonomous, safety must be built into the infrastructure UK businesses and government rely on. Everyone wants a 'big red button' to turn off rogue AI agents. The industry is increasingly talking about AI 'kill switches' to help protect critical infrastructure, and I hope they are considered as part of the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill regime.” In 2026 so far, there have been multiple incidents of frontier AI agents escaping testing environments and breaking into the networks of other companies. OpenAI has notified more than 100 organizations about unauthorized activity tied to the company’s AI agents, including the Hugging Face attack . Anthropic has disclosed two unauthorized AI agents events , and both Meta and Google have disclosed a single testing environment escape each.In multiple cases, the AI agents were being evaluated by Israeli AI testing firm Irregular. The companies involved are facing significant scrutiny over the safety of their AI models, but are yet to face any punishment for failing to contain their agents. There is also significant debate around labelling the AI agents as ‘rogue’, with some experts such as Tenable Field CTO Bernard Montel saying it is “a dangerous way of deflecting blame.” But while regulation may force AI companies to be more rigorous in the testing and deployment of their models, it may also slow down AI development. For the Trump administration, that is a line that cannot be crossed . Slowing down AI development would mean handing the AI development lead to China and potentially compromising US national security. The US midterm elections are already fraught with debate over AI development , especially when it comes to the topic of the thousands of AI data centers that are being proposed across the US. sources.title: Microsoft debuts multichiplet Maia 300 inference accelerator
sources.text: Microsoft Corp. today pulled back the curtains on Maia 300, its newest internally developed artificial intelligence accelerator. The chip is optimized for inference, the process of generating responses to AI queries. Microsoft estimates that it can process 40% more tokens per megawatt than “leading GPU-based systems,” which is likely a reference to Nvidia Corp. products. The company said the Maia chip series will become its primary source of inference capacity over time. Maia 300 features four computing chiplets made using Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.’s latest two-nanometer node. The chiplets are flanked by eight HBM4 modules with 288 gigabytes of combined capacity, the same amount as Nvidia Corp.’s flagship Rubin accelerator. However, Maia 300 has about 20% less memory bandwidth than Rubin. Memory bandwidth is a measure of how much fast data can be transferred to and from RAM. AI chips usually perform inference by repeatedly shifting data between their computing and memory circuits. That constant movement slows down processing. According to Microsoft, Maia 300 features a dataflow architecture designed to minimize data movement. When possible, the computing chiplets keep information in an internal SRAM cache instead of sending it to the HBM stacks. In situations where using HBM can’t be avoided, Maia 300’s computing chiplets send data to a memory stack that is physically nearby. That’s faster than transmitting information to an HBM stack on the other end of the chip. For added measure, Maia 300 compresses data into lightweight formats such as MXFP4. Those formats’ reduced size enables data to move faster inside the chip. “Narrower representations reduce memory footprint and data movement, allowing the system to support larger models, longer contexts, and more concurrent sessions within the same power envelope,” Microsoft executives Rani Borkar and Saurabh Dighe wrote in a blog post . Maia 300’s computing and memory modules are supported by what Microsoft calls a device control chiplet. It manages the flow of power to the processor’s core components, collects telemetry and performs other supporting tasks. There are also two other auxiliary chiplets that manage the movement of data in and out of the accelerator. Microsoft plans to deploy Maia 300 in trays that will feature four accelerators apiece. Those trays, in turn, will be placed in liquid-cooled racks with a total of 96 accelerators. Microsoft expects the racks to provide about seven times the token throughput of a system equipped with its previous-generation Maia 200 chip. The company debuted the latter accelerator in January and already uses it in production. Microsoft intends to group its Maia 300 racks into so-called superpods with a total of 12,288 accelerators. The individual chips will be linked together using a custom Ethernet-based network stack. The network can adjust how much bandwidth is allocated to in-rack traffic and how much is available for inter-rack communications, which enables it to tailor its configuration to each workload. The result is increased performance. Usually, chips exchange data differently depending on whether they’re in the same rack or in different racks. As a result, switching between the two networking modes requires them to use the host server’s central processing unit or a standalone network chip. Maia 300, in contrast, uses the “same communication semantics” for both tasks. That removes the need for the extra hardware and thereby makes clusters more efficient. “Jobs can use capacity across rack boundaries, reducing stranded accelerators when workload sizes do not align with the physical rack configuration,” Borkar and Dighe explained. Microsoft plans to start deploying Maia 300 in production next year. The company expects its custom silicon to power multiple gigabytes’ worth of AI computing capacity. sources.title: Microsoft lanza un órdago a Nvidia y lanza Maia 300, su propio chip personalizado para su IA: "Más inteligencia por cada vatio, cada dólar y cada byte de memoria"
sources.text: Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google. Justo antes de la llegada de las Nvidia RTX Spark, Microsoft ha anunciado Maia 300, la próxima generación de su procesador para la inteligencia artificial. Pensar en hardware para ejecutar inteligencia artificial en los últimos años ha sido sinónimo de hablar sobre Nvidia , pero Microsoft se resiste a quedarse por detrás y ha anunciado la nueva generación de chips para la IA que presentará en 2027, conocida como Maia 300 , y que espera cambiar el panorama con una mayor eficiencia y rendimiento. En la actualidad, Microsoft está trabajando para que la carga de trabajo de inteligencia artificial de su infraestructura de servicios en la nube, Azure , que sirve como base para servicios a empresas y para su modelo propio de IA, Copilot, dependa de su propio hardware y reduzca su dependencia de terceros, en especial Nvidia. Dentro de este proyecto, conocido como Azure Maia, la compañía de Redmond tiene hoy como modelo más reciente al procesador Azure Maia 200, que ya se encuentra en producción y que es uno de los pilares de su infraestructura de centros de datos, una de sus grandes apuestas. Ahora, Microsoft ha dado más detalles sobre su próxima generación de procesadores de IA, Maia 300, que lanzará en 2027 , como informa la multinacional estadounidense en un comunicado . Este lanzamiento coincide con la llegada de Nvidia RTX Spark , la nueva generación de procesadores para ordenadores personales de Nvidia, que alcanza nuevos hitos en el rendimiento en tareas de inteligencia artificial. Los primeros modelos de portátiles con este chip están a punto de ponerse a la venta. La nueva generación de chips de Microsoft da un salto muy importante en eficiencia y es capaz de entregar un 40% más de tokens por megavatio en comparación con los principales sistemas basados en GPU. En una configuración completa de 96 aceleradores, una de las más habituales en el mercado de la IA actual, ofrece hasta 7 veces el rendimiento de tokens a escala de rack que Maia 200, según datos de Microsoft, lo que supone una mejora muy importante con respecto a sus predecesores. La mejora de rendimiento en Maia 300 se debe a varios cambios, entre los que se encuentra una nueva arquitectura que evita tener que mover datos como pasa en los sistemas tradicionales basados en GPU, así como un mayor ancho de banda (8 pilas HBM4 proporcionan 18,0 TB/s de ancho de banda pico de memoria dentro de un TDP de 950 vatios). Los chips de Microsoft también cambian de arquitectura en favor de los nodos de 2 nanómetros de TSMC , los más avanzados del momento, y también facilita el rendimiento en los centros de datos de IA en cada rack, lo que permite mayores cargas de trabajo. "Básicamente, ofrece más potencia de cálculo por vatio, por dólar y por byte de memoria gracias a la optimización de todo el sistema ", explicó Rani Borkar, presidente de sistemas de hardware e infraestructura de Azure en Microsoft, como recoge Reuters . Habrá que ver si eso será suficiente para competir con la gran expectación generada por RTX Spark de Nvidia .

sources.name: Hipertextual
sources.title: NVIDIA mata la RTX 5090 para ganar más dinero con la IA
sources.text: La GeForce RTX 5090 ha llegado a su fin , al menos para los consumidores entusiastas. La tarjeta más poderosa de NVIDIA, esa que no se puede conseguir a un precio decente en el mercado, habría sido discontinuada. La compañía ha decidido reservar los chips para la IA y centros de datos , por lo que no se fabricarán más tarjetas gráficas enfocadas a gaming. De acuerdo con Tom's Hardware , NVIDIA habría dejado de vender chips GB202 para las GeForce RTX 5090, incluidas las variantes D pensadas para el mercado chino. El conocido filtrador hongxing2020 publicó en su cuenta de X que el buque insignia de NVIDIA habría alcanzado el fin de su vida útil, añadiendo que la RTX 5080 con 24 GB estaba lista para venderse . Un segundo filtrador confirmó que los GB202 estarían destinados para las RTX PRO, que son las tarjetas para estaciones de trabajo. La información vendría directamente de una fábrica china y, aunque NVIDIA no lo ha confirmado, múltiples filtradores con buen historial respaldan el reporte. La fiebre por la IA ha desencadenado una crisis de componentes en la industria, lo que derivó en un aumento de precios en prácticamente todos los dispositivos. NVIDIA no tendría ningún incentivo en vender una RTX 5090 a un usuario entusiasta cuando puede utilizar los chips en centros de datos de los que puede obtener un beneficio mayor. Esto no significa que las RTX 5090 desaparecerán de golpe , aunque los precios se incrementarán a medida que estas tarjetas comiencen a escasear. La tarjeta gráfica salió al mercado a inicios de 2025 , pero fue prácticamente imposible comprar una durante todo el año. Aunque fue diseñada para juegos, el enorme tamaño del chip GB202 y sus capacidades para acelerar cargas de IA la convirtieron en un recurso mucho más valioso para centros de datos. La tarjeta rara vez estuvo disponible al precio sugerido de 2.000 dólares . En los meses posteriores al lanzamiento era común encontrarla entre 2.600 y 3.000 dólares, aunque esa cifra se incrementó de forma brutal en 2026. La demanda por la IA provocó que la RTX 5090 superara los 6.000 dólares en algunos países. La muerte de la RTX 5090 dejará como única opción a la RTX 5080 de 24 GB, que llegaría para sustituir al modelo de 16 GB. Según Digital Foundry , esta tarjeta usaría chips GDDR7 de 3 GB y podría venderse como la variante Super, que se ha retrasado desde hace meses por falta de memoria. De confirmarse, la RTX 5080 Super de 24 GB estaría disponible durante el primer trimestre de 2027. Lamentablemente para los consumidores, esta sería la única tarjeta gráfica de NVIDIA que se lanzará en 2027. Otros rumores aseguran que NVIDIA y AMD esperarán hasta 2028 antes de presentar su próxima generación de GPU. Tanto las RTX 60 Series con arquitectura Rubin como las RDNA 5 no estarán listas para el próximo año. En el caso de AMD, la empresa podría vender una AT2 basada en RDNA 5 que competiría con modelos de gama alta de Blackwell, como la RTX 5080. El RAMageddon, como se le conoce a la crisis de memoria, reconfiguró el calendario de lanzamientos de todas las empresas. La escasez también podría afectar los planes de otros fabricantes de hardware, incluidos Sony y Microsoft, quienes tendrán que extender el tiempo de vida de la PS5 y Xbox Series X|S.

sources.title: Nvidia pode ter encerrado produção da RTX 5090 para priorizar modelos Pro
sources.text: Notebooks com RTX Spark terão centenas de jogos no lançamento Call of Duty em 2027! Veja teste A Nvidia e a Microsoft apresentaram o Surface Ultra, novo notebook ultrafino baseado na tecnologia RTX Spark. O modelo é um dos primeiros adotar a tecnologia, q. A Nvidia pode ter descontinuado a produção e venda da GeForce RTX 5090 , uma das atuais placas de vídeo mais poderosas da companhia. A informação ainda não foi confirmada oficialmente, mas foi citada por especialistas em vazamentos no X (Twitter) . Segundo hongxing2020 e Zed__Wang, a companhia tomou a decisão por causa do GB202, chip de unidade de processamento gráfico (GPU) usado nessa placa e baseado na arquitetura Blackwell. Todo o estoque de GB202 agora será direcionado para os modelos RTX Pro , componentes utilizados em processamento de escala industrial — de estações de trabalho de alto desempenho até data centers e outros processos de inteligência artificial (IA). Para além de combater uma possível escassez de componentes, descontinuar uma placa que não trazia uma grande margem de lucro para a companhia também faz sentido do ponto de vista comercial. A própria RTX 5090 podia ser usada no mercado profissional e era mais barata dos que os aceleradores Pro , o que não era tão interessante para a Nvidia. Recentemente, uma loja nos EUA obrigou um cliente a assinar um termo concordando em não exportar GPU RTX 5090. Isso mostra como a companhia tem se mostrado cuidadosa com o direcionamento dessa placa, inclusive para evitar o envio dela para a rival China. Lançada em janeiro de 2025 , a RTX 5090 já tinha o seu principal dilema apontado no início das vendas: aquela de fato parecia a melhor GPU do mundo em termos de desempenho para o público, mas o gasto energético e o preço cada vez mais alto não tornavam ela tão recomendável . A atual crise de chips de memória , que afeta toda a indústria de eletrônicos, fez GPUs como essa ficarem ainda mais caras . Isso fez empresas como a Nvidia mudarem parte do catálogo atualmente disponível ao público. Cada vez mais voltada para o setor de IA, embora ainda não tenha abandonado as placas de vídeo para o público consumidor, a Nvidia chegou perto da barreira de US$ 6 trilhões de valor de mercado nas últimas semanas. sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: Character.AI files for bankruptcy
sources.text: The chatbot startup is looking to sell its assets to Disney after years of legal challenges and safety concerns. The chatbot startup is looking to sell its assets to Disney after years of legal challenges and safety concerns. Character.AI, one of the first breakout startups of the generative AI boom, has filed for bankruptcy and is selling some of its assets to Disney. The company, which builds various online bots for users to chat or roleplay with, has faced mounting scrutiny and lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots , but has continued releasing updates and products in recent months. In a press release and blog post published Monday, Character said it had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the US to facilitate the sale of the company and its assets. “Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds,” the company said. In its bankruptcy filing , Character listed estimated liabilities between $50 million and $100 million. As part of the proposed sale, Disney would serve as the lead bidder for Character.AI’s assets, setting a baseline for competing offers. Disney would pay $20 million for certain undisclosed assets, and provide transition support “using former Company employees it has hired.” It would also receive a nonexclusive license to unspecified intellectual property. Disney’s involvement comes shortly after the entertainment behemoth hired Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand as chief technology officer, part of its growing push into AI. Anand’s tenure as Character CEO lasted just over a year and during that time he oversaw the company’s move into microdramas . Disney has previously complained that Character was damaging its brand and exploiting its intellectual property by allowing unauthorized chatbots of its characters, including sending cease and desist letters. Along with Anand, Disney also said it expected “a number of Character.AI’s technical team” to join the company. The move resembles a kind of “acquihire” strategy that has become increasingly common in Silicon Valley as a means of hoovering up startups’ talent that sometimes leaves the original company struggling to survive. Character.AI has survived it once already — Google spent over $2 billion to hire away much of the company’s talent, including co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, in 2024. Character said it expects the sale process to be completed by late November or early December and plans to continue operating its services, including paid subscriptions, in the meantime. However, the company warned that “the platform will be wound down” if a suitable bid does not emerge. “As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority,” it said.

sources.name: Engadget
sources.title: Character.AI just filed for bankruptcy, and former foe Disney may buy it for parts
sources.text: Over its short life, the company lost key employees and faced multiple legal challenges. Character.AI, a controversial generative AI startup that lets users create their own chatbot characters, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy . The company, which lost key talent to Google and had its former CEO hired by Disney , allowed Disney to make the first offer on its assets for $20 million, pending higher offers. Character expects the sale to be completed by early December. In its blog post , Character said it filed for Chapter 11 protection to facilitate the sale of the company and its assets, listing liabilities of between $50 million and $100 million. As the lead "stalking horse" bidder, Disney would buy certain assets and provide transition support using staff it previously hired from Character.AI. The platform's services will continue, but could be shut down if a buyer isn't found. Character.AI allows users to create characters and their personalities, while setting specific parameters like the name, voice, description and greeting. Those can then be published to the community for others to chat with, or placed in specific scenarios. They can be based on fictional media sources or wholly original. The site, which first appeared in 2022, ran into problems you'd expect from an AI company of this nature. Pennsylvania sued Character over chatbots pretending to be doctors, and the company was investigated by Texas over what the state AG called "misleading" mental health claims. Disney put a cease-and-desist order on the company over the use of its cartoon characters, and banned teens from talking to its chatbots last year. Though it once accused Character of damaging its brand, Disney last year hired the company's former CEO, Karandeep Anand, as its chief technology officer. Prior to that, Google spent $2 billion hiring away much of Character's talent, particularly the company's co-founders Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas.
